translations.title: How big should your emergency fund be, and where should it sit?
translations.excerpt: Three months for a dual-income salaried couple, nine for the self-employed, and never in the same account you spend from.

blocks.text: An emergency fund is the money that stops a bad month from becoming a bad decade. It covers a job loss, a hospital deposit, a parent's surgery or a car that dies on the highway, without touching investments or taking a personal loan at 16%.
Count essential expenses only: rent, EMIs, food, utilities, school fees, insurance premiums. Streaming subscriptions and weekend plans pause in an emergency.

items: One month in a savings account you do not spend from day to day.
The rest in a sweep-in fixed deposit or a liquid mutual fund; both pay more than savings interest and can be withdrawn within a day.
Not in equity funds, gold or your PPF; prices fall at the worst moments and lock-ins defeat the purpose.

blocks.text: A credit card limit is not an emergency fund. It is an emergency loan at roughly 40% a year.

items: Size it on essential expenses, not total spending.
Keep it liquid and boring: savings account, sweep-in FD, liquid fund.
Refill it before restarting SIPs after you use it.
